input:
In this example, we are going to take a closer look at a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves an ice rink, and we are going to work out how its actual performance stacks up against the very best performance that could theoretically be achieved under exactly the same conditions. The unit in question operates with an evaporating temperature of −25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C, which are fairly typical sort of values for this kind of application.

Because the Carnot coefficient of performance has to be calculated using absolute temperatures, the first step is essentially just to convert the two Celsius values onto the absolute scale. When we do this, we find that the evaporating temperature comes out at 248.15 K, while the condensing temperature comes out at 308.15 K. The temperature lift across the unit, in other words the difference that the machine has to work against, is therefore 60 K. The Carnot coefficient of performance is simply the evaporating temperature divided by this lift, and plugging the numbers in gives us a value of 4.13 for this particular duty, which represents the absolute reversible limit.

In practice, of course, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of just 1.75, a figure that comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. This achieved value inevitably sits below the Carnot value, largely because the Carnot figure assumes a perfectly reversible cycle, whereas a real machine inevitably suffers from pressure drops in the circuit, losses in the compressor, and throttling rather than work-producing expansion, all of which drag the performance down. It is also important to bear in mind that part-load performance is not stated anywhere here, so this particular comparison is really only a full-load comparison at the end of the day.
target:
Determine the Carnot coefficient of performance of a vapour-compression unit serving an ice rink, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C, and set the installed unit against that limit. The Carnot coefficient of performance is calculated from the absolute temperatures, so the two Celsius values are converted first. The evaporating temperature is 248.15 K. The condensing temperature is 308.15 K. The temperature lift across the unit, the difference the machine must work against, is 60 K. The lift is set by the duty the rink imposes, not by the machine, and the lift is the quantity against which the cycle performance is measured. The Carnot coefficient of performance is the evaporating temperature divided by the lift, and the relation thus gives 4.13 for this duty.

The installed unit achieves 1.75. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load. The achieved coefficient of performance stands below the Carnot value, and the gap is the expected one: the Carnot figure assumes a reversible cycle, and the installed machine departs from that ideal through pressure drops in the circuit, losses in the compressor and throttling in place of work-producing expansion, each of which lowers the coefficient of performance below the reversible limit. The comparison is a full-load comparison only. Part-load performance is not stated, and no coefficient of performance at part load can be read from the figures given. At full load, the installed unit delivers a little under half of the reversible performance available between the same two temperatures, and any judgement of the machine is a judgement of that gap and of nothing else.
